title: The Girl Who Fed the Dark
summary: Every night, Sabra feeds the darkness under her bed so it won't grow hungry and take the whole house. But the more she feeds it, the bigger it gets — and she must learn what the dark is truly starving for, and why feeding a fear only makes it grow.

chapters.title: The Thing Under the Bed
chapters.body:
Sabra was nine, and there was a darkness under her bed, and she was the only one who knew how to keep it fed.

It had started small. When she was very little, the dark under her bed had been just an ordinary dark — the harmless shadow any bed casts. But one night, lying awake, Sabra had felt it change. She'd felt it become aware. Become hungry. A cold, watchful, patient hunger, gathered in the black space beneath her, and she had known — the way children sometimes know things grown-ups have forgotten how to know — that if the hunger grew great enough, the dark would rise up out from under the bed and swallow the whole room, and then the whole house, and everyone sleeping in it.

So Sabra had learned to feed it.

She discovered, by trying, what the dark would take. It would not take food — she'd tried leaving bread and it stayed till morning, untouched. What the dark ate was other things. It ate her nightlight, when she left it burning down under the bed — by morning the little light would be dead, its glow eaten, and the dark would be quiet and full for a night or two. It ate her courage, if she lay very still and let herself be afraid and pushed the fear down into the dark — the dark drank fear like milk, and grew calm. It ate the small brave things about her, one by one, and in exchange it stayed under the bed and didn't rise up and swallow the house.

Every night, Sabra fed it. She gave it her nightlight, so she slept in true blackness. She gave it her fear, lying rigid and terrified until the dark had drunk its fill. She gave it, over the months, the little brave nighttime things a child has — the courage to get up for a glass of water, the courage to check a strange noise, the courage to sleep with the door open. One by one she fed them to the dark, to keep it quiet, to keep it from growing hungry enough to take everything.

And it worked. Sort of. The dark never rose up and swallowed the house. Every morning, everyone was safe. Sabra told herself she was protecting them — that she was the brave one, the one who kept the hungry dark fed so it wouldn't hurt anyone. It was a heavy secret to carry for a nine-year-old, feeding a darkness every single night, but she carried it, because she believed she had to.

There was only one problem, and it frightened her more each night, though she tried not to think about it.

The dark was getting bigger.

The more she fed it, the larger it grew. When she'd started, the hungry dark had filled only the space directly under her bed. Now it had spread — she could feel it — to the whole underside of the bed, and creeping out along the floor, and some nights she felt it lapping at the edges of her blanket, bigger and hungrier than ever, needing more each night to stay quiet. She was feeding it everything she had, and instead of being satisfied, it was growing. And Sabra was running out of brave things to give it.

chapters.title: What the Dark Was Starving For
chapters.body:
One night, when Sabra had almost nothing left to feed it — no nightlight, no courage, nearly no brave things remaining — the dark under her bed grew so large and so hungry that it began, at last, to rise.

She felt it come up over the edge of the mattress, cold and vast and starving, larger than her whole room, and she knew she had failed — she had run out of things to feed it, and now it would take everything. In her terror, Sabra did something she had never dared to do in all the months of feeding it. She spoke to it.

"Please," she whispered into the rising black. "I don't have anything left. I've fed you everything. My light, my courage, all my brave things. Why are you still hungry? Why do you keep getting bigger? What do you want?"

And the dark, for the first time, answered her — not in words exactly, but in a cold vast feeling that pressed into her mind, and what it said astonished her.

I want what you keep feeding me, it said. More. Always more. You taught me to eat your courage, and so courage is what I hunger for, and the more you feed me, the more I crave. Every brave thing you give me makes me bigger, and every bit bigger I get, the hungrier I am. I will never be full, child. That was never possible. The more you feed a hunger like mine, the greater it grows. You have been making me bigger every single night, and calling it keeping me small.

Sabra lay frozen in the rising dark, and a terrible understanding broke over her. She had been feeding the dark to keep it from growing. But the feeding was what made it grow. Every scrap of courage she'd given it hadn't satisfied it — it had enlarged it, taught it to want more, fed the very hunger she was trying to quiet. She'd had it exactly backward. The dark wasn't a thing you kept small by feeding. It was a thing that grew on being fed. And the more frightened she'd been, the more she'd fed it, and the more she fed it, the bigger and hungrier it got, and the more frightened she became — around and around, a wheel that only ever turned one way: toward a darkness that swallowed everything.

And she understood something else, in that frozen moment — the deepest part of it. The dark ate courage. It grew on fear. Which meant the dark was not really a monster under the bed at all. It was her fear itself, given a shape and a hunger. The thing she'd been feeding every night was the very fear of it — and fear is exactly the kind of thing that grows the more you feed it, and shrinks only when you refuse to. Every night she'd lain rigid and terrified and pushed her fear down into the dark, she'd thought she was getting rid of the fear. But she'd been feeding it. Growing it. Making the very thing she was afraid of larger with her own fear of it.

The dark loomed over her, vast now, filling the room, starving as it had never been — because she had fed it so well, for so long, that it had grown almost too big to satisfy.

And Sabra realized that there was only one thing she had never tried. In all the months of feeding the dark, of giving it her courage and her light and her brave things, she had never once done the opposite. She had never refused to feed it. She had never faced it with the one thing that might actually make it shrink.

chapters.title: The Night She Stopped Feeding It
chapters.body:
The dark hung over Sabra, huge and cold and starving, waiting for her to do what she always did — to be afraid, to feed it her terror, to give it one more scrap of courage and make it, once again, a little bigger.

And Sabra, lying in the vast black with almost nothing left, made the hardest choice of her small life. She decided to stop feeding it.

It was terrifying. Every instinct screamed at her to be afraid, to push the fear down into the dark, to feed it and appease it as she always had. But she understood now that the feeding was the trap. So instead of giving the dark her fear, she held onto it. She lay in the enormous starving blackness, more frightened than she had ever been, and she did not push the fear away, and she did not feed it to the dark. She just held it. Felt it. Let herself be afraid, fully afraid, without giving the fear away to the thing under the bed.

And she said, out loud, in a voice that shook but did not break: "No. I'm not going to feed you anymore. I'm scared — I'm so scared — but I'm going to keep my fear. It's mine. And I'm going to keep my courage too, what's left of it. You don't get any more of me. Not tonight. Not ever."

The dark surged, furious, and pressed down on her, and for a moment Sabra thought it would swallow her whole. It was so big, and she was so small, and every part of her wanted to give in, to feed it, to make it calm the only way she knew.

But she didn't. She held her fear, and held her ground, and refused to feed the dark — and something began to happen.

The dark, unfed, began to shrink.

It was slow at first. But the vast starving blackness, denied the courage it fed on, denied the fear it grew from, began to draw back. Deprived of the only thing that made it larger, it could not stay large. It pulled back from the edges of her blanket. It shrank down off the mattress. And the more it shrank, the less frightening it became, and the less frightened Sabra grew — and the less frightened she grew, the less there was to feed it, and the more it shrank. The wheel that had only ever turned one way was turning the other way now: toward a darkness that dwindled, because she had stopped feeding it, because a fear you refuse to feed cannot help but starve.

Smaller and smaller the dark drew, back under the bed, back into the shadow, back down into the ordinary harmless dark that any bed casts — until there was nothing under Sabra's bed at all but the plain, quiet, empty dark of a normal night. The hunger was gone. The monster was gone. It had never been anything, she understood now, but her own fear, grown huge on a diet of her own feeding — and once she stopped feeding it, it had nowhere to grow, and nothing to be.

Sabra lay in her bed in the ordinary dark, still shaking a little, still holding her fear — but holding it, now, instead of feeding it away. And she found that fear you hold onto is a strange thing: it doesn't grow. It just sits with you a while, and then, when you don't feed it, it quiets on its own, and shrinks, and finally rests. The fear that had ruled her nights for months had never needed to be fed and appeased. It had needed only to be faced, and held, and refused.

She slept, that night, with no nightlight, in the plain dark, unafraid — not because the dark was gone, but because she finally understood it. And she never fed it again.

In the mornings after, Sabra got her brave things back, one by one — the courage to get up for water, the courage to check a strange noise, the courage to sleep with the door open. They came back because she stopped giving them away. And she was, everyone said, a notably brave child after that, braver than most grown-ups, though no one knew why. Only Sabra knew. She had learned the thing that most people spend their whole lives not learning: that a fear is not a monster to be fed and appeased, growing bigger with every scrap you give it. It is a hunger that lives on being fed, and dies on being refused. You do not keep the dark small by feeding it your courage. You keep it small by holding your ground, and holding your fear, and refusing — even when you're terrified, especially when you're terrified — to give it one more bite.
